A1.justification: Both PDFs describe HASS, with matching authors, core methods, and original experiments despite the changed title. Text, equations, tables, and figures support comparison throughout. v1 ends with references and has no appendix; v3 includes readable Appendices A.1–A.8.

before.justification: v1 reports original acceptance-length and speedup experiments on three LLaMA models, alongside loss-weight, alignment-step, and teacher-generated-data studies.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds original experiments on a 70B model, translation, alternative losses, training-data quantities, and computational overhead.

M1.justification: The default Top-K loss, feature-alignment procedure, architecture, and inference remain unchanged. v3 introduces exploratory training adaptations: weighting step j's loss by beta^(j-1) in Section 4.2.3 and replacing training tokens with draft-generated tokens in Appendix A.2. The expanded formulation and pseudocode primarily document the existing method.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates dialogue, code generation, and mathematical reasoning through MT-bench, HumanEval, and GSM8K. v3 retains these and adds German, French, Japanese, Russian, and Chinese translation into English, using draft models without translation-specific adaptation (Appendix A.7, Table 11). This substantially expands task and language coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 add vanilla speculative sampling with Vicuna-68M and LLaMA-68M drafts, plus Medusa, to the retained LLaMA2 comparisons. Table 3 compares Top-K loss against six alternatives, including BiLD and Recall@k Surrogate loss. Appendix A.4 also adds EAGLE-2 to the self-distillation comparison that v1 reported only for HASS.

E3.justification: v3 adds the LLaMA3-Instruct 70B configuration, training-data fractions from one-eighth to the full dataset, drafting-depth/token-budget grids, and controls for loss weighting and token replacement. Appendix A.8 introduces training profiling on one H800 with batch size 2. The original inference metrics, temperatures, batch size, and default HASS settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's loss-hyperparameter and alignment-step studies, v3 tests alternative losses, early-versus-late step weighting, feature versus token alignment, drafting budgets, and sensitivity to training-data scarcity. It expands the existing self-distillation study across models and comparators and measures training overhead. These directly examine design choices, failure cases, and practical costs.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. v3's averages across tasks and average/peak GPU-memory measurements do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Matched entries in Tables 1–2 and the alignment-step table (v1 Table 3; v3 Table 4) retain their values. v3 adds substantial results: for example, 70B mean HASS speedups are 4.05x and 3.85x at temperatures 0 and 1, versus EAGLE-2's 3.37x and 3.28x. Translation, new baselines, ablations, and resource measurements provide further new findings, rather than improved scores under the original settings.

T1.justification: Appendix A.8 adds mathematical reasoning about training cost: attention work accumulates with the sum of alignment-step indices, other work scales with the step count, and backward cost is approximated as 2(A+O). This refines v1's simple n-fold-overhead statement. The Top-K equation is unchanged, and the expanded Section 3.2 formulation mainly restates the existing procedure; no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains harmonizing training objectives and contexts for acceleration without additional inference overhead. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion extend validation from three to four LLaMA models and update the claimed speedup range from 2.81x–3.65x to 2.81x–4.05x, and the advantage over EAGLE-2 from 8%–15% to 8%–20%.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations of the trade-off between early and later speculation steps, suggests training-task mismatch explains weak self-distillation results on code/math, and interprets data-scarcity experiments as evidence of better data exploitation. It also explains drafting-depth versus verification-cost trade-offs and distinguishes measured training time from FLOPs and memory, substantially refining v1's efficiency discussion.

D1.justification: v1 provides core hyperparameters and the upstream EAGLE-2 repository. v3 adds a HASS-specific code URL, training and attention pseudocode, explicit identification and access information for ShareGPT's 68,000 dialogues, teacher-response generation instructions, and training throughput/FLOPs/memory information. These substantially expand documentation without establishing changes to the retained implementation.

R1.justification: v3 adds Medusa, BiLD, Recall@k Surrogate loss, and Yi et al.'s multilingual speculative-decoding work, while removing Cascade Speculative Drafting and Online Speculative Decoding references. The central positioning around aligned training, efficient decoding, and EAGLE/GLIDE's context mismatch remains. Publication updates to retained references are bibliographic changes.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled 'Learning Harmonized Representations for Speculative Sampling.' The abstract and substantial introductory, preliminary, and methodological prose are rewritten, with context inconsistency moved ahead of objective mismatch in the motivation. Expanded method explanations and an organized eight-part appendix substantially develop the exposition, although the main section sequence remains.

P2.justification: Tables 1–2 and Figures 1 and 5 expand to accommodate additional comparisons and the 70B model. v3 adds tables for losses, reweighting, token alignment, self-distillation, drafting settings, data scarcity, and translation, plus Figures 6–11 and pseudocode displays. The architecture illustrations persist, and v1 Table 3 becomes v3 Table 4 without numerical changes.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation of HASS's design and practicality. Alternative-loss and alignment controls address choices only lightly tested in v1, while Appendix A.8 replaces an undifferentiated overhead claim with measured time, computation, and memory costs. Broader comparisons and translation tests support applicability, and implementation disclosures improve reproducibility. Discussion of unsuccessful variants and limited self-distillation gains clarifies trade-offs. Repeated-run uncertainty remains absent, but the gains in empirical support and transparency are substantial.
